Neonatal Eptesicus serotinus emerge weighing approximately 5.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.8 grams], a modest birth mass typical of insectivorous bats that rely on substantial maternal investment during the early postnatal period. Field data indicate that although pups are born altricial, they progress rapidly through the suckling stage. Under the thermal conditions typical of active roosting periods at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the interval from birth to weaning is notably brief, lasting approximately 24 days [tx = approximately 24 days]. This compressed suckling duration reflects the high metabolic demands placed on both mother and offspring in temperate environments, where the growing season for insect prey is sharply limited. Following weaning at a body mass of around 14.8 grams [Wwx = around 14.8 grams], the young bats enter a juvenile phase characterized by intensive foraging practice and flight skill development. The comparatively low weaning mass relative to adult values suggests that the nutritional independence transition occurs before full somatic growth is achieved.

Female Eptesicus serotinus exhibit a reproductive strategy that balances a single annual litter with a modest litter size, typically producing one to two pups per litter [N_R_i = one to two pups per litter]. This annual reproductive output, defined as one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], is relatively low compared to many small vespertilionids, which may produce multiple litters within a single breeding season. The gestation period of 68 days [tg = 68 days], recorded under controlled colony conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], is consistent with the duration observed in other medium-sized congeneric species and appears to be constrained by the energetic costs of maintaining pregnancy during the spring emergence period when ambient temperatures and insect availability fluctuate unpredictably. Such a gestation length allows parturition to be timed with peak seasonal insect abundance, thereby enhancing neonatal survival prospects. The investment in a small number of relatively well-developed pups per reproductive event is a life-history trait shared with many temperate-zone bats.

The species achieves an ultimate wet weight ranging from 20 to 30 grams in healthy, free-ranging adults, with a typical asymptotic body mass of 25 grams [Wwi = 25 grams]. This range in adult body size is partially attributable to geographic variation and seasonal fat deposition patterns, as individuals in more northerly populations often attain greater pre-hibernation masses. Comparative data for Eptesicus serotinus suggest that adult body mass is an important determinant of overwinter survival, with heavier individuals exhibiting higher rates of recapture following hibernation. The observed maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated from banding returns at approximately 21 years [am = approximately 21 years], recorded in individuals maintained under conditions that approximate a body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during the active season. This lifespan is among the longest documented for European bats of comparable body size and reflects the slow life-history pace typical of the order Chiroptera, where extended lifespans are coupled with low annual reproductive output.

Sexual maturation in Eptesicus serotinus occurs relatively late in the context of temperate bats, with puberty estimated to occur at 547 days [tp = 547 days] after birth under the thermal conditions characteristic of active-season metabolism at 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This value, originally documented for the closely related congener Eptesicus fuscus, is considered broadly applicable to E. serotinus owing to their similar body size, thermal physiology, and life-history scheduling. The extended juvenile period enables young bats to refine foraging proficiency and accumulate the fat reserves necessary for their first hibernation before committing energy to gonadal development. The cessation of reproductive activity in older females is not well documented, but senescence effects on pregnancy success and litter size have been noted in long-term maternity colony studies. The delay in pubertal onset is a common pattern among bats, in which delayed reproduction is offset by greater adult survival.

The estimated maximum reproductive rate in Eptesicus serotinus reflects the inherent constraints of producing a single annual litter with a maximum of two pups. Under the thermal conditions of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], each female typically produces one to two pups per litter [N_R_i = one to two pups per litter] and one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], yielding a modest annual fecundity that typifies the order Chiroptera. In free-living populations, actual reproductive output is often lower than this theoretical maximum, as annual pregnancy rates in monitored maternity colonies rarely exceed 80 percent and may decline still further during years of poor insect availability. Foraging habitat quality, roost microclimate, and maternal body condition collectively modulate the realized reproductive rate. The species' slow reproductive tempo is compensated by exceptionally high adult survival probabilities, resulting in stable population dynamics across much of its temperate Palearctic range. Life-history theory predicts that such a combination of low fecundity and extended lifespan arises in environments where juvenile mortality is unpredictable but adult survival can be reliably maintained.
